text: The data model is the "where does the data come from" half of every BI Publisher report. Let's go one level deeper: data sets, parameters, and the XML every template eventually consumes.

A data model is built from one or more data sets, each essentially a query returning the rows and columns the report needs. In Fusion Financials, that's commonly built against predefined view objects or an existing subject area, though SQL-based data sets are supported too. A report might have one data set for a simple list, or several combined, a header data set for company info plus a detail data set for invoice lines.

A data model can define parameters, values a user supplies before the report runs, a date range, a business unit, a minimum dollar amount. Parameters flow into the query as filter conditions, so the same report runs for different slices without anyone editing the underlying query. This mirrors the point-of-view concept from Financial Reporting Studio.

When there's more than one data set, they're typically linked, a detail set filtered by the same invoice ID as its header set, so the combined XML nests detail rows correctly beneath their header. Getting this structure right matters, because a template can only lay out the shape of XML it's actually given.

Whatever the sources, the end result is always XML, a self-describing hierarchy of tags. You can preview that XML directly from the data model, and that's exactly how a template gets built. Up next, lesson seventeen: report templates.
